rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Al-Razi rejects the commentators’ claim that reversed pair order merely follows verse endings: Qur'anic wording carries sound meaning, unlike rhyme-driven poetic rearrangement.
rows.anchor: فيكون اللفظ حاملا له على تغيير المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before Muhammad's mission, disbelievers were like the blind and their path darkness; after it, those guided to faith became seeing and their path light, so the earlier state is named first.
rows.anchor: الكفار قبل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كانوا في ضلالة فكانوا كالعمى وطريقهم كالظلمة ثم لما جاء النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In describing the final return, shade precedes scorching heat because mercy is given precedence over wrath, as the report says, “My mercy precedes My wrath.”
rows.anchor: قدم ما يتعلق بالرحمة على ما يتعلق بالغضب لقوله في الإلهيات سبقت رحمتي غضبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The living are believers who accepted God's revelation; the dead are those who heard clear verses but gained no benefit, and are placed after the believers because their spiritual death followed the believers' life.
rows.anchor: أي المؤمنون الذين آمنوا بما أنزل الله والأموات الذين تليت عليهم الآيات البينات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blind are mentioned before the seeing because the misguided disbelievers existed before the believers guided after the mission.
rows.anchor: وقدم الأعمى على البصير لوجود الكفار الضالين قبل البعثة على المؤمنين المهتدين بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blind/sighted and shade/scorching heat are compared as kinds rather than individuals: particular members can match or surpass one another, while the difference between the kinds is certain.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر الأفراد لأن في العميان وأولى الأبصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Living and dead are plural because the gap is absolute: no dead person equals any living person in perception, whether kinds or individuals are compared.
rows.anchor: ما من ميت يساوي في الإدراك حيا من الأحياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth is one—the affirmation of God's oneness—whereas falsehood has many forms of associating partners, including worship of planets, fire, and idols shaped like angels; hence darkness is plural and light singular.
rows.anchor: الحق واحد وهو التوحيد والباطل كثير وهو طرق الإشراك على ما بينا أن بعضهم يعبدون الكواكب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explaining the singular “light” and plural “darkness,” al-Razi refers back to his account of “He made darknesses and light” and says light requires an illuminant, a receptive place, and no barrier; without any one, darkness remains.
rows.anchor: السبب في توحيد النور وجمع الظلمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sunlit house needs an opening for the rays and a receptive surface; if the light passes through an opposing opening into another room, the first room can remain dark, illustrating the three conditions for illumination.
rows.anchor: إذا حصلت الأمور الثلاثة يستنير البيت وإلا فلا تتحقق الظلمة بفقد أي أمر كان من الأمور الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reading contrasts divine and prophetic hearing: God can make the dead hear, while the Prophet cannot make buried people hear; the disbelievers likewise cannot hear his recitation and revelation.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد بيان كون الكفار بالنسبة إلى سماعهم كلام النبي والوحي النازل عليه دون حال الموتى فإن الله يسمع الموتى

words: وما أنت بمسمع من في القبور
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the verse consoles Muhammad: only God can make them hear, even if they were deaf rocks, so he bears no responsibility for their response.
rows.anchor: وأما أنت فلا تسمع من في القبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Muhammad only a warner explains and reinforces the consolation that he cannot make the stubborn hear.
rows.anchor: إن أنت إلا نذير } بيانا للتسلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse continues evidence for God's power and will by surveying composite creation: animals and non-animals, with plants nobler than minerals, followed by animals; the earlier mention of fruit and mountains represents plants and minerals.
rows.anchor: قسم دلائل الخلق في العالم الذي نحن فيه وهو عالم المركبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans head the animal list as its noblest kind. Beasts precede livestock either because their benefits are enjoyed while alive whereas livestock are eaten, or because “beast” conventionally includes the horse, nobler than other animals after humans.
rows.anchor: لأن منافعها في حياتها والأنعام منفعتها في الأكل منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine singular description is used because humans are included among the subjects, and masculine wording is more elevated and apt.
rows.anchor: فذكر لكون الإنسان من جملة المذكورين

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of the one feared grows with knowledge of him: the scholar knows God and therefore fears and hopes in him.
rows.anchor: الخشية بقدر معرفة المخشي ، والعالم يعرف الله فيخافه ويرجوه

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars outrank worshippers because honor is measured by piety (49:13), and piety in turn by knowledge; honor thus depends on knowledge rather than deeds, though a scholar's failure to act calls his knowledge into question.
rows.anchor: فبين أن الكرامة بقدر التقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's might and retribution evoke complete fear, while his forgiving what is lesser evokes abundant hope.
rows.anchor: كونه عزيزا ذا انتقام يوجب الخوف التام ، وكونه غفورا لما دون ذلك يوجب الرجاء البالغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the reading that puts “scholars” in the accusative and “God” in the nominative, the sense is that God is magnified and revered.
rows.anchor: بنصب العلماء ورفع الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This warning is linked by conjunction to the promise for those who recite God's Book; the intervening passage concerns those reciters, and on one view the mention of gardens of Eden also refers back to them.
rows.anchor: وما بينهما كلام يتعلق بالذين يتلون كتاب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are not allowed the relief of death; their punishment continues without end.
rows.anchor: أي لا يستريحون بالموت بل العذاب دائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike worldly pain, the afterlife's torment neither kills its victims nor becomes familiar to a body until it is no longer felt; it remains severe at every moment and the punished remain in it.
rows.anchor: بل هو في كل زمان شديد والمعذب فيه دائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence stresses that torment is neither ended nor eased: even death, its strongest possible end, is withheld, so they will wish for death without receiving it.
rows.anchor: لا ينقطع ولا بأقوى الأسباب وهو الموت حتى يتمنون الموت ولا يجابون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the punished, it is enough to say their torment will not diminish; by contrast, the blessed are promised an increase from God's bounty.
rows.anchor: في المثابين ذكر الزيادة بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing the message, the passage states resurrection as another of the three principles that make a morally responsible person a believer and Muslim.
rows.anchor: لما بين الرسالة وهو أصل من الأصول الثلاثة التي يصير بها المكلف مؤمنا مسلما ذكر أصلا آخر وهو الحشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the full reward and punishment promised in the warning and glad tidings are not visible in worldly life, God will resurrect people and reward those warned and those given good news.
rows.anchor: فالله يحيي الموتى ويجزي المنذرين ويجزي المبشرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Resurrection is also offered as confirmation of the preceding description of fearing the All-Merciful unseen.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر خشية الرحمن بالغيب ذكر ما يؤكده وهو إحياء الموتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One parsing makes “We indeed” a subject and predicate, like a famous person identifying himself simply as “I”; God is known by his perfect attributes, so his self-identification suffices.
rows.anchor: أن يكون مبتدأ وخبرا كقول القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “We” is emphatic and “give life” is the predicate; al-Razi prefers this parsing.
rows.anchor: كأنه قال إنا نحيي الموتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase signals God's oneness: unlike people who need names and lineage to distinguish them from namesakes, God has no partner from whom he must be distinguished; thus message, oneness, and resurrection are all stated.
rows.anchor: ليس غيرنا أحد يشاركنا حتى تقول أنا كذا فنمتاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes “what they sent ahead” to include both what they did earlier and what they left for later, with one side of the pair stated alone, as in clothing that protects from heat while cold is also intended.
rows.anchor: فاكتفى بذكر أحدهما كما في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading is the good or bad deeds they sent ahead into existence.
rows.anchor: المعنى ما أسلفوا من الأعمال صالحة كانت أو فاسدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third possibility is that what is recorded as sent ahead is their intentions, which precede their deeds, while their traces are the deeds themselves.
rows.anchor: نكتب نيانهم فإنها قبل الأعمال

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The traces may be footprints: when Companions whose homes were far from mosques considered moving, the Prophet told them to remain, saying God records and rewards their steps.
rows.anchor: إن الله يكتب خطواتكم ويثيبكم عليه فالزموا بيوتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Traces can also be lasting good practices (such as books, bridges, and charitable endowments) or bad practices (such as misleading books and instruments of vice), which bring reward or liability to their originators.
rows.anchor: كالكتب المصنفة والقناطر المبنية

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says whoever establishes a good practice receives its reward and the reward of those who follow it without reducing theirs, while whoever establishes an evil practice bears its burden and the burden of those who follow it.
rows.anchor: من سن سنة حسنة فله أجرها وأجر من عمل بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation identifies the traces as deeds and what was sent ahead as intentions, which come before deeds.
rows.anchor: ما ذكرنا أن الآثار الأعمال وما قدموا النيات فإن النية قبل العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although writing precedes resurrection in time, resurrection is named first because it is the central purpose: without resurrection for reckoning, writing is not significant, and without revival the record has no effect.
rows.anchor: الكتابة معظمة لأمر الإحياء لأن الإحياء إن لم يكن للحساب لا يعظم والكتابة في نفسها إن لم تكن إحياء وإعادة لا يبقى لها أثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic “We indeed” conveys majesty; resurrection, God's uniquely great act, is therefore stated before the lesser act of writing, which further magnifies it.
rows.anchor: الإحياء عظيم يختص بالله والكتابة دونه فقرن بالتعريف الأمر العظيم

words: وكل شيء أحصيناه في إمام مبين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says the record confirms that people's deeds and traces are fixed in advance: God first wrote what they would do, then records it when they do it.
rows.anchor: فإن القلم جف بما هو كائن

words: وكل شيء أحصيناه في إمام مبين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the phrase assures preservation: unlike notes that can be lost, what God records is kept in a clear register.
rows.anchor: نكتب ونحفظ ذلك في إمام مبين

words: وكل شيء أحصيناه في إمام مبين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view generalizes from deeds and traces to every thing: no word or act escapes God's knowledge or is lost from the record.
rows.anchor: شيئا من الأقوال والأفعال لا يعزب عن علم الله ولا يفوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We enumerated it” is stronger than “We wrote it,” because scattered writing would still require collecting and totaling what was recorded.
rows.anchor: لأن من كتب شيئا مفرقا يحتاج إلى جمع عدده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The register is called an imam because angels follow its instructions about lifespan, provision, revival, and death.
rows.anchor: وسمي الكتاب إماما لأن الملائكة يتبعونه فما كتب فيه من أجل ورزق وإحياء وإماتة اتبعوه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative identification of the clear register is the Preserved Tablet.
rows.anchor: وإمام جاء جمعا في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Imam” can be singular, like “book” and “veil,” or plural, like “mountains” and “ropes”; al-Razi reads the form in 17:71 as plural, “their leaders.”
rows.anchor: فإمام إذا كان فردا فهو ككتاب وحجاب وإذا كان جمعا فهو كجبال وحبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Clear” means that the register manifests to angels what they must do and to people what will be done to them; it also distinguishes the creatures' outcomes, separating the people of Paradise from those of the Fire.
rows.anchor: والمبين هو المظهر للأمور لكونه مظهرا للملائكة ما يفعلون وللناس ما يفعل بهم وهو الفارق يفرق بين أحوال الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After treating two of the three principles, oneness and resurrection, the passage turns to the third, prophethood: oneness appears in the ban on serving Satan and the command to worship God, and resurrection in the scenes of Hell and sealed mouths.
rows.anchor: وههنا ذكر الأصلين الوحدانية والحشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying God did not teach Muhammad poetry indicates that God teaches him what He wills and does not teach what He does not will.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أنه معلم من عند الله فعلمه ما أراد ولم يعلمه ما لم يرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse singles out poetry because Muhammad's opponents called him a diviner when his reports of the unseen came true, a magician when he performed miracles, and a poet when he recited the Qur'an; only the Qur'an was his challenge to them, so poetry is denied specifically.
rows.anchor: ما كان يتحدى إلا بالقرآن

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: One reported interpretation is that poetry did not come naturally to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: قال قوم ما كان يتأتي له

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that poetry did not come easily to him, so any verse he attempted would have defective meter.
rows.anchor: وآخرون ما يتسهل له حتى أنه إن تمثل بيت شعر سمع منه مزاحفا

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says that when Muhammad recited the line “And news will come to you from one you did not provide for,” its meter was defective, offered as evidence that poetry was not easy for him.
rows.anchor: كان يقول صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi prefers the plain sense that poetry does not befit Muhammad: a lawgiver's wording follows the intended meaning, whereas a poet's meaning follows diction chosen first to satisfy meter or rhyme.
rows.anchor: على مفهومه الظاهر وهو أن الشعر ما كان يليق به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry is metered speech whose meter is intended primarily; if a speaker aims first at meaning and the result happens to be metered and rhymed, it is not poetry.
rows.anchor: الشعر هو الكلام الموزون الذي قصد إلى وزنه قصدا أوليا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 3:92 is not poetry although it can be scanned in a poetic meter: the wise person seeks the meaning first, while a poet selects words first to fit the meter and makes meaning follow them.
rows.anchor: لن تنالوا البر حتى تنفقوا مما تحبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad's occasional utterance of a metrical line, including “I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of Abd al-Muttalib,” does not make him a poet because he did not intend meter and rhyme first; even much accidentally metrical speech would not do so.
rows.anchor: أنا النبي لا كذب … أنا ابن عبد المطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary market speech can scan as a poetic meter without being poetry, since its speakers did not first intend the wording for meter or rhyme.
rows.anchor: إذا تتبعت كلام الناس في الأسواق تجد فيه ما يكون موزونا واقعا في بحر من بحور الشعر ولا يسمى المتكلم به شاعرا

words: إن هو إلا ذكر وقرآن مبين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast is between the Qur'an as reminder and admonition aimed at meaning and poetry as speech embellished by rhyme and meter.
rows.anchor: هو ذكر وموعظة للقصد إلى المعنى

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said that some poetry contains wisdom: a poet may intend wording and happen upon a wise meaning, while a sage may intend meaning and happen upon meter; neither thereby becomes the other kind of speaker.
rows.anchor: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ( إن من الشعر لحكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meaning is the heart and spirit of wording, while wording is its form; a sage's metrical speech remains wisdom, and a poet's admonition may convey wisdom, so meter does not negate the message's substance.
rows.anchor: قلب اللفظ وروحه فإذا وجد القلب لا نظر إلى القالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb has a tāʾ reading that addresses Muhammad and a yāʾ reading that is either about Muhammad or the Qur'an; the former yāʾ interpretation is closer in meaning and the latter closer in wording.
rows.anchor: خطابا مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وبالياء على وجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With yāʾ, the Prophet can be the one warning, referring back to him in the preceding verses; al-Razi judges this closer in meaning.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المنذر هو النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حيث سبق ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the Qur'an itself can be the subject of “warn”; this reading is closer to the wording because the Qur'an is the nearest antecedent.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد أن القرآن ينذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Alive” may mean alive in God's knowledge, destined to be guided by the warning.
rows.anchor: من كان حيا في علم الله فينذره به فيؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it means alive in reality, that is, a believer who is warned of punishment for sins and reward for obedience.
rows.anchor: لينذر به من كان حيا في نفس الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The word becomes due” can mean God's sentence of punishment after a messenger has come, including the decree to fill Hell; punishment then falls on those who denied the messenger.
rows.anchor: أما قول العذاب وكلمته كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it refers to the statements about oneness, prophethood, resurrection, and the other foundational doctrines, whose proofs the Qur'an provides.
rows.anchor: وأما القول المقول في الوحدانية والرسالة والحشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After threatening idol worshippers, God promises those who avoid worshipping idols and shirk; pairing promise with threat throughout gives full encouragement and warning.
rows.anchor: من اجتنب عبادتها واحترز عن الشرك

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: The Kashshaf author derives ṭāghūt from ṭughyān on the pattern faʿalūt, with metathesis that puts the root's lām before its ʿayn.
rows.anchor: الطاغوت فعلوت من الطغيات كالملكوت والرحموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi lists emphatic force in treating the verbal noun as the thing itself, using an intensive pattern (as in vast mercy and expansive dominion), and reversing the root letters.
rows.anchor: في هذا اللفظ أنواع من المبالغة أحدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Putting the root's lām before its ʿayn is an unusual word formation chosen only for emphasis.
rows.anchor: إنما يصار إليه عند المبالغة
